title: The Wizard Who Forgot to Return
markdown:
The crystal ball wobbled, and a stone slipped from beneath it.

Wizard Aster caught it before it hit the cottage floor. Not just any stone. This one pulsed with a faint inner light, like a captured firefly. “Oh, fiddlesticks and fireflies,” he said, voice a little shaky. “This is the Whispering Stone. I borrowed it from the Mountain King for a tricky spell last fortnight, and completely forgot.”

Nettle, a cat as sleek and black as midnight, with eyes like two perfect pieces of polished amber, flicked an ear. Her amber gaze met Aster’s. Well, Wizard, you know what must be done now, don’t you?

High amongst the jagged peaks, where the earth breathed warm sighs through vents in the black rock, Aster’s snug cottage smelled of herbs and warm milk. It sat beside meadows of soft grey ash that shimmered like moon dust. Aster was a wizard with clever spells and an even cleverer mind, and a rather endearing habit: he borrowed things. Little things, always with the best intentions. A bright feather for a potion, a gleaming shard of mica for a charm, a whisper of wind in a jar. He always meant to return them. Sometimes they got misplaced in his wonderfully cluttered mind, tucked away like a forgotten acorn. Nettle had chosen him, sensing a kindred spirit in his gentle fussiness. She understood the language of a sigh and the meaning of a misplaced teacup.

Aster sighed, a sound like rustling autumn leaves. “Indeed, Nettle. I must return it before His Majesty misses it. And without him even realising it was ever borrowed.” The very thought made his whiskers twitch.

He began packing his satchel. First, a collapsible telescope. “One must observe the terrain,” he muttered. Then a warming charm. “The air up there can be frightfully chilly,” he explained to Nettle, who blinked slowly, unimpressed. Next he tucked away a book of etiquette, open to The Proper Return of Borrowed Sparkle-Stones with Minimal Fuss. Nettle watched from her perch, tail giving a slow amused sway.

Their journey took them up winding paths, past steaming vents that puffed clouds of white steam. The ash meadows gave way to slopes of sharp obsidian and ancient craggy basalt. Aster kept glancing at his compass, then his map, then his book. He adjusted his spectacles, a nervous habit.

“Now, Nettle,” he whispered, voice strained. “We must be discreet. The Mountain King is a creature of considerable pride. We’ll simply place the stone near his throne when he’s looking the other way, and then, poof. We’ll spirit away. Easy peasy, lemon squeezy.” He even attempted a smile, which looked more like a grimace.

Just then a deep rumble echoed. A colossal figure emerged from behind boulders: Grok, the ogre shepherd, draped in rough wool. His face, though ogre-like, was surprisingly thoughtful as he guided his flock of shaggy mountain goats, their bells tinkling.

Aster froze, hand instinctively reaching for his satchel. Nettle simply sat down, calmly observing Grok. She seemed to sense something unexpected.

“Greetings, wizard,” rumbled Grok, voice like stones rolling downhill, yet pleasant. “And to your feline companion. A fine day for a stroll amongst the peaks, wouldn’t you agree?”

Aster, taken aback by the ogre’s geniality, stammered, “Ah, good day, Grok. A fine day indeed, yes. Very lofty.” He clutched the Whispering Stone in his pocket, its warmth pressing insistently against his palm.

Grok paused, brow furrowing slightly. “You seem a trifle flustered, Wizard Aster. Has something been borrowed and not yet returned, perhaps?”

Aster’s jaw dropped. His facade crumbled. “W-well, I…” he began, voice trailing off into a squeak.

Nettle let out a soft knowing purr. Honesty, Wizard. It’s less taxing.

Grok chuckled, a sound that vibrated through the ground. “Fear not, kind sir. It is no shame to borrow; it is often a sign of appreciation. And returning something with a bit of flourish, that’s where the true art lies.” He gestured with a large gentle hand. “Allow me. The Mountain King values respect, and the proper presentation of gifts. A hurried surreptitious return is like a wildflower snatched from its stem. It loses its fragrance, does it not?”

Aster blinked. His plans of stealth dissolved like mist. He had not prepared for an ogre lecturing him on etiquette. He glanced at his book, then at Grok’s earnest face, feeling a blush creep up his neck.

Just then a magnificent sight caught Aster’s eye. Further up the slope, a colossal dragon was curled into a slumbering coil. Its scales were the colour of smouldering embers, a soft golden light radiating from its immense form. It stirred slightly, a slow blink of an ancient intelligent eye, then settled back to its nap, utterly unconcerned. It radiated an aura of patient waiting.

Grok followed Aster’s gaze, a faint smile touching his lips. “Ah, old Ignis,” he murmured. “She enjoys the warmth of the earth. A wise creature; she knows patience. She understands that some things are best observed with a quiet heart.”

Aster took a deep breath, the dragon’s peaceful presence settling his nerves. He looked at Grok, at the sincere look in the ogre’s eye, and then at Nettle, who gave him an encouraging blink. “You are quite right, Grok,” Aster said, voice steadier. “And my preparations were perhaps a trifle excessive. I have the Whispering Stone right here.” He pulled it from his pocket. It felt heavier now, not with magic, but with his own realisation.

“It is a truly beautiful stone,” Grok said, gaze admiring, not with avarice but with genuine appreciation. “And it belongs to the King, of course. But how will you present it? Not merely tossed over the castle wall, I trust, like a common pebble?”

Aster smiled, genuine this time. “No, Grok. Not tossed. Perhaps I could offer it with a rather apologetic bow and a sincere explanation. And perhaps a small gift of appreciation for your own excellent counsel. A story, perhaps, told with the setting sun.”

Grok’s broad face broke into a wide genuine smile. “An excellent notion. Honesty, delivered with courtesy and a touch of grace, is a treasure in itself. And as for a gift, a story would be most welcome indeed when I return to my hearth this evening. The goats appreciate a good tale, too, you know.”

And so, with Grok’s jovial guidance, Aster approached the Mountain King’s obsidian castle. He did not sneak. He walked with Nettle by his side, the Whispering Stone held carefully in his palm, presented, not hidden. He explained, with a slight blush, his absentmindedness and his intention to return it with all due respect. The Mountain King, a stern but fair ruler, listened. He did not scold. Instead he nodded slowly, a flicker of amusement in his gaze.

“A valuable lesson learned, Wizard Aster,” he declared. “You have, indeed, shown true courtesy.” Grok, standing proudly beside Aster, gave a satisfied grunt.

Back in their warm cottage, the comforting scent of simmering stew filled the air. Old Elara and young Finn had gathered for their usual evening get-together. The ash meadows outside were dusted with the first light of evening stars. Aster, no longer fussing, shared the tale of his day, of Grok’s unexpected wisdom and the dragon’s quiet majesty. Nettle, curled on Aster’s lap, purred contentedly. There was no grand feast. Just the gentle murmur of conversation, the clinking of mugs, and the comforting glow of the hearth. Aster stroked Nettle’s sleek fur and did not reach for the etiquette book. The stone was back where it belonged. So, for once, was he.
characters: Aster (an absentminded borrowing wizard), Nettle (a sleek amber-eyed cat)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
